name: Carlos Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What happens on a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos Diaz, 58, and I moved from print-shop maintenance into line work after a vocational certificate. I'm still junior at the electricity company: I load fittings, help build and repair lines, and ask Gabriel to watch my difficult climbs; I love solving a visible fault, though I tire sooner than younger hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology fit into that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an approved AI assistant every day to quiz myself on equipment and tidy rough notes. Gabriel and the training manual check what it says before I use anything at a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the AI assistant saves me ten minutes of writing, which is pleasant, but the repair is still on us. A pole doesn't become safe because my notes are neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I'm almost glad for an uneventful run, because I need another few seasons to become a good lineworker. I switched from print-shop maintenance at 55, and our higher pay plus a year's expenses saved let me practice without a weekly money panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking supervised field calls and use the approved AI assistant each evening to quiz me on the day's equipment. In the first year I'd compare every answer against the training manual with my mentor before trying anything at a live site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel easy about the work and a little restless. My partner Noor and I have grown children living elsewhere, so the kitchen table has space for my manuals now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the assistant get wrong recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It mixed up two insulator ratings when I described a wet pole. My mentor Gabriel caught it in the manual, and I wrote the correction in my own notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you like climbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the view after a repair is finished, but I still watch Gabriel's feet to learn where he places them. A late starter shouldn't pretend height is routine.

say: I'd say **AI notes** save time after a repair call.
I'd remind the crew that **pole safety** still depends on people at the site.
think: I need **more field seasons** to become a good lineworker.
Our **year of savings** and higher pay make that learning period affordable.
do: Keep **supervised field calls** and use the approved assistant to quiz equipment each evening.
Check **AI answers** against the manual with Gabriel before using them on site.
feel: **At ease** about income, with a little impatience to improve.
S0.quote: A late starter shouldn't pretend height is routine.
fieldNote: Carlos uses **AI daily** as a study aid but has seen it confuse insulator ratings and checks the manual.
His **strong reserve** lets him focus on gaining competence after a late move from print-shop maintenance.

steps.text: Continue supervised line calls while learning foot placement from Gabriel
Use the approved AI assistant for daily equipment quizzes checked against the manual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that faster buying could stop us waiting all morning for a fitting, if the software knows what's actually on the shelf. I'd invite the storekeeper to test it before treating her job as optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My field work seems safe for now, but fewer dispatch delays might also mean fewer paid callouts for me. Noor runs a small catering service, and quicker booking tools could help her, though I won't budget for extra orders that haven't arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to join the approved stock-checking trial and log every mismatch between the screen and the shelf. In the first year, if my callout pay falls, Noor and I will delay buying a second catering van and keep using the hired one for busy weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the stock tool and cautious about the money. A trial is something I can test; a forecast of our household pay is much softer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the last stock mismatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen said there were six insulated clamps; the box held four and two ordinary clamps. The storekeeper found the correct pair in a return tray before the truck left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hire the van rather than buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor only needs it for large weekend orders. A monthly loan payment would stay even if my callouts or my partner Noor's catering orders dropped.

say: I'd support **stock trials** with the storekeeper before staffing changes.
I'd welcome **faster buying** when shelf counts are accurate.
think: My **callout pay** could shrink even if field repairs continue.
Noor's **catering orders** may grow or fall, so I won't count imagined income.
do: Join the **stock-check trial** and record screen-versus-shelf mismatches this month.
Delay a **second catering van** if callout income drops in the first year.
feel: **Curious** about the tool, cautious about household pay.
S1.quote: A monthly loan payment would stay even if my callouts or my partner Noor's catering orders dropped.
fieldNote: Carlos sees **stock efficiency** as useful, but connects tighter scheduling to a realistic loss of his own extra pay.
The **hired van** gives the household flexibility while Noor's catering orders and his callouts remain uncertain.

steps.text: Join the approved stock-checking trial and log shelf mismatches
Delay buying a second catering van if callout pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 changes our plans and ordering first, while repair robots follow around 2031. We should test them on a wet, awkward pole before cutting any repair shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031 I may still need my wage, and a junior could be the easiest person to remove. We have a year's expenses saved and several utilities nearby, but I can't assume their inspection teams will need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask for the utility's robot trial criteria and start a log of field situations that drawings miss. In 2029 I'd take a funded equipment-testing course if offered; in the first robot year I'd apply for paid testing or inspection roles at our company and nearby utilities, keeping line shifts until a real offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keyed up, not frozen. I'm willing to learn the machines early, but I can't manufacture a paid place to use that skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What field situation belongs in the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Willow Lane pole has a bird nest behind the crossarm that hides a cracked brace. A camera looking only from the road could miss it, so I'd document the angle Gabriel used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor say about applying elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Noor would want travel time and wages on paper before I accept anything. Her catering clients are here, and we wouldn't move just because a vendor promised new jobs.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd require **wet-pole trials** before repair shifts are cut.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when junior posts shrink.
A **year of savings** and nearby utilities help without guaranteeing inspection work.
do: Request **robot trial criteria** and log field hazards missing from drawings now.
Take a **funded testing course** if offered in 2029, then apply for paid testing or inspection work.
feel: **Keyed up** and willing to learn, without assuming a vacancy exists.
S2.quote: I can't manufacture a paid place to use that skill.
fieldNote: Carlos eagerly collects **robot trial evidence**, yet distinguishes a possible testing job from an actual offer.
His **local job search** must fit Noor's catering clients, so he checks travel and wages before any move.

steps.text: Take a funded equipment-testing course in 2029 if offered
Apply for paid robot-testing and inspection jobs at nearby utilities
Keep paid line shifts until a real replacement offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers five years is enough to run a real field trial, including failures, not just a polished demonstration. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and hands-on repair robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 66 when robots can repair lines, and retirement may be affordable, but I haven't checked the numbers with Noor yet. The extra time could also let me become a useful tester, although I know the thinking AI may do some monitoring itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get a written retirement forecast and ask Gabriel to review my fault log. In 2032 I'd apply for a paid field-testing rotation if the company opens one; in the first robot year I'd choose between a real testing shift and retirement after comparing both with our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel engaged rather than rushed. Five years lets me try the equipment and still make a decision from actual numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which numbers matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor's catering income swings by season, and our roof needs work. We'd compare a low-income season with the retirement estimate before dropping my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the rotation is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep regular line shifts while I can and revisit the retirement budget. I'm not going to buy a private robot course on a guess.

say: I'd ask for **failure reports** in every field trial.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from 2034 repair robots.
think: At **66**, retirement might work after a low-income catering season is included.
A **testing role** is possible, but monitoring itself may be automated.
do: Get a **written forecast** and have Gabriel review the fault log this year.
Apply for a **paid field-testing rotation** if offered in 2032, then compare real shifts with retirement costs in 2034.
feel: **Engaged** and less rushed, with decisions tied to actual numbers.
S3.quote: I'm not going to buy a private robot course on a guess.
fieldNote: Carlos's **2034 choice** depends on a real testing offer and a retirement budget that includes Noor's seasonal income.
He will not **self-fund speculative training**, despite his comfort with new technology and early trial work.

steps.text: Compare a written retirement estimate with roof costs and low catering income
Apply for a paid field-testing rotation in 2032 if offered
Keep regular line shifts if no testing rotation opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger crew members to learn the old feeder maps alongside the new machines, because ten years is time to make a decent handover. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots in 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to be retired from climbing before 71, provided the written numbers cover our bills and Noor's catering income is treated cautiously. I don't expect my junior field job to be a safe place once robots can do it, even with all the years to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep earning lineworker wages and add to my fault log after each unusual call. In 2037 Noor and I would set a retirement date if our low-season budget works; in 2039 I'd give the training team the Willow Lane photographs and repair notes for new workers and robot operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our near-term income and grateful for time to plan. I would still hate for a younger worker to inherit a beautiful map with the wrong view of a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful handover look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Willow Lane photos show the brace from above and behind the bird nest, where the crack actually sits. I'd label the angle and the date so a trainee can check it on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the low-season budget fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid work or apply for a real inspection vacancy and postpone retirement. Our grown children have their own expenses, and I won't turn their visits into a request for money.

say: I'd ask younger crews to learn **feeder maps** and new equipment together.
I'd mark **2039 robots** as the field change, when I'll be 71.
think: I may retire before **71** if conservative household figures support it.
My **junior field role** won't stay safe once robots can repair lines.
do: Keep **paid line work** and add unusual faults to my log.
Set a **2037 retirement date** if the low-season budget works; hand over Willow Lane records in 2039.
feel: **Calm** about current income and grateful for planning time.
S4.quote: I would still hate for a younger worker to inherit a beautiful map with the wrong view of a pole.
fieldNote: Carlos's likely **retirement before 2039** rests on a conservative budget, not on treating the distant robot date as permanent job safety.
His **fault log** is meant for a specific handover, with camera angle and repair date preserved for new workers.

steps.text: Continue paid line work and record unusual field faults
Choose a 2037 retirement date only if low-season income covers bills
Apply for a real inspection vacancy if retirement figures fall short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because repair robots arrive in 2031 while I may still need the wage. Funded testing training, real paid vacancies, wet-weather trials and honest staffing numbers would help me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who records the bad trials as carefully as the successful ones. A machine can look perfect on a clear day and still miss the cracked brace behind a nest.

headlineQuote: A machine can look perfect on a clear day and still miss the cracked brace behind a nest.
portrait: Carlos is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who entered from print-shop maintenance and still learns difficult climbs from Gabriel.
His **year of savings** let him test tools, while Noor's seasonal catering income shapes household decisions.
He uses **AI daily** for study and notes but checks ratings and field instructions against manuals and experienced workers.
The **2031 repair robots** worry him most because training may not lead to a paid testing or inspection post.
Longer warning supports **field trials**, with detailed fault photographs for later crews.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Carlos most because 2031 robots could reach his field job while he still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **funded testing training**, real paid vacancies, wet-weather trials and honest staffing numbers.
